Hi!
I'm Vanda Miravent and I'm a new user of DISTANCE 3.5.

My study has the aim to estimate relative densities of song birds by
the method and statistical theory proposed by JŠrvinen and VŠisŠnen (
1975 in Oikos).
I understood that in this method they collect data field in transepts
with two belts: 0 to Y and Y to infinity and to estimate the
detectability and density of a specie they use the proportion of birds
detected within the belt 0 to Y relatively to the total number of
birds detected in the two bands.

My question is:

- DISTANCE 3.5 allow to analise data collected in that way and estimate
densities using that proportion of birds detected in the two belts?

- If yes, how to introduce data recorded in interval Y to infinity and
how to define its interval in the program



Thank You ,



Vanda Miravent

messages.author: a52219e2e622d1af
messages.subject: Re: (no subject)
parts:
> > My study has the aim to estimate relative densities of song birds by
> > the method and statistical theory proposed by JŠrvinen and VŠisŠnen (
> > 1975 in Oikos).
> > I understood that in this method they collect data field in transepts
> > with two belts: 0 to Y and Y to infinity and to estimate the
> > detectability and density of a specie they use the proportion of birds
> > detected within the belt 0 to Y relatively to the total number of
> > birds detected in the two bands.
> >
> > My question is:
> >
> > - DISTANCE 3.5 allow to analise data collected in that way and estimate
> > densities using that proportion of birds detected in the two belts?

Yes - at least approximately. You need to replace 'infinity' by some
large value w - and the analysis will probably be rather more robust if
you don't make that value too large. Say w=100m for woodland/forest,
larger for more open habitat.

> > - If yes, how to introduce data recorded in interval Y to infinity and
> > how to define its interval in the program

Just record them all at any distance larger than Y - say Y+1 m. Then in
the 'intervals' tab of the data filter, define 2 intervals, one from 0 to
Y, the other from Y to w. (Note: for distances in the 1st interval,
record them as any value between 0 and Y - say Y/2.)

Note that you will only be able to fit one-parameter models - the
half-normal without any adjustment terms, or the uniform with one
adjustment term - and you won't be able to test whether the model fits the
data with just 2 intervals.

Steve Buckland
